title: GST_122 — End of Semester Objective Exam
guideTitle: GST_122 — Communication in English Language II

questions.q: Chidi plays a chapter of an audiobook and afterwards jots down its main ideas. Which of the four language skills was he chiefly using while the chapter played?
questions.concept: Classifying a scenario to a language skill
questions.why:
Listening is the ability to understand, interpret and respond to spoken language. An audiobook reaches him as sound, so following it is listening, exactly as summarising a TED Talk is.

Reading is the trap because a book is involved, but nothing was read as written text; jotting the ideas down afterwards is writing, and no speaking takes place.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six components of effective speaking (oral communication)?
questions.why:
The six components are clear pronunciation, appropriate tone, the ability to engage the audience, voice control, body language and delivery. An extensive vocabulary is not among them: communication is about expressing ideas effectively, not about big words.

Voice control, body language and appropriate tone are all on the list, so choosing one of them means the six were not learned.

questions.q: A passage describes a market at dawn: the colours of the fabrics, the smell of frying akara, the calls of the traders. It tells no story and argues for nothing. Which writing style is this?
questions.why:
The four writing styles are persuasive, descriptive, narrative and expository. Descriptive writing paints a detailed picture of a person, place or thing through sensory detail, which is all this passage does.

Narrative needs events in sequence; persuasive takes a side and pushes the reader to agree; expository explains a topic rather than picturing it.

questions.q: A presenter pronounces every word clearly and her argument is sound, but she slouches, keeps her eyes on the floor and never gestures. Which component of effective speaking is she failing?
questions.why:
Posture, eye contact and gesture are body language, one of the six components of oral communication, and that is what she neglects.

Pronunciation is stated to be fine; voice control concerns pitch, pace and volume of the voice itself; appropriate tone concerns whether the manner suits the occasion.

questions.q: What is the one thing that turns hearing into listening?
options: Meaning is processed and a response formed
The sound is loud enough to notice
The sound comes from a person rather than a machine
The sound lasts more than a few seconds
questions.why:
Hearing is the bare reception of sound; listening adds understanding, interpretation and response, which is why it is defined as the ability to understand, interpret and respond to spoken language.

Loudness, source and duration do not matter: a generator running outside all night is heard, not listened to, and a whispered instruction can be listened to closely.

questions.q: A persuasive speech on assisted suicide is built from these parts: (1) ethical considerations on the other side; (2) a statement of the speaker's position; (3) historical context; (4) arguments in favour. In which order should they come?
questions.why:
The introduction states the position. The body then gives the historical context, the arguments in favour (personal autonomy, compassion, reducing suffering) and finally the ethical considerations on the other side (sanctity of life, potential for abuse), so that both sides are covered: 2, 3, 4, 1.

Opening with context buries the position; 2, 4, 3, 1 argues before setting the context; 2, 3, 1, 4 gives the opposing view before the speaker's own case instead of after it.

questions.q: Students who fake anxiety in order to obtain deadline extensions cause classmates with genuine anxiety to be met with disbelief and stigma. Which of the four key takeaways about faking mental health issues does this describe?
questions.concept: Key takeaways on faking mental health issues
questions.why:
Undermining Legitimacy: faking diminishes the legitimacy of genuine cases and perpetuates stigma, and here a genuine sufferer is disbelieved because of the fakers.

Misallocation of Resources is about treatment and professional attention being diverted; Obstructing Access to Support is about help being blocked from those who need it; Honesty and Understanding is the positive takeaway that promoting honesty ensures authentic sufferers receive care.

questions.q: Effective communication is a matter of expressing ideas clearly rather than reaching for elaborate vocabulary. On that understanding, what do good grammar and careful word choice contribute?
options: Credibility, better problem-solving and closer attention to detail
An impressive vocabulary that stands in for clear ideas
A guarantee that every listener will take the message identically
Delivery skills such as voice control and body language
questions.concept: Why grammar and word choice matter
questions.why:
Communication is about expressing ideas effectively, not about big words. Grammar and word choice still matter because they increase credibility and improve problem-solving and attention to detail.

The second option is the very error the point corrects; identical uptake by every listener is impossible because meaning must be interpreted by the receiver; voice control and body language are components of oral delivery, not of grammar.

questions.q: In which sentence is 'snake' used in its denotative sense only?
options: That salesman is a real snake.
The zoo keeps a snake in a glass tank.
Beware of him, he is a snake in the grass.
Her snake of a brother sold the family land.
questions.why:
Denotative meaning is the literal, dictionary meaning: a snake is a legless reptile, and the zoo sentence means exactly that.

The other three use the connotative meaning, the implied sense of a treacherous person, which carries emotional and cultural associations. Test: D for Dictionary, C for Culture.

questions.q: Which of these written sentences still has two distinct readings even on the page?
options: Their car is in the garage.
questions.why:
'I saw her duck' can mean the bird she owns or the act of ducking; the sentence is ambiguous, and writing it down does not settle it.

The other three contain hazardous homophones (their/there, principal/principle, bare/bear) that could mislead a listener, but once spelled out each has only one reading. Their confusion is sound-based, which is the mark of a homophone, not ambiguity.

questions.q: A driver stops at a red light, a customer recognises a bank by its logo, and a hotel guest obeys a no-smoking pictogram. The study of how such signs and symbols carry meaning is called:
questions.why:
Semiotics is the study of signs and symbols, their interpretation and their role in communication; communication is not solely about words.

Syntax is sentence structure, concord is grammatical agreement, and connotation is the implied meaning of a word, not a field of study.

questions.q: A manager praises the sales team as 'aggressive', then checks how colleagues from other countries might take that word before sending the message company-wide. Which competency is he showing?
questions.why:
Cultural Sensitivity is awareness that connotations vary across cultures, which is exactly what he is checking.

Semiotic Awareness concerns signs and symbols rather than words; Clarity in Expression is phrasing so that only one meaning is available; Conflict Resolution reconciles a discrepancy after a misunderstanding has already happened.

questions.q: Standing beside a river, Musa hears 'the bank is closed' and uses the setting to decide that the speaker means the riverbank, not a place that keeps money. Which competency is this?
questions.why:
Contextual Interpretation is reading meaning in the light of the situation: the river fixes which sense of 'bank' is intended, which is the active interpretation that multifaceted meaning requires of a listener.

Semiotic Awareness would be noticing a sign or symbol; Cultural Sensitivity concerns connotations varying across cultures; Clarity in Expression is the speaker's job, not the listener's.

questions.q: Which pair names the two sources of confusion that stand in the way of conveying meaning accurately?
questions.concept: The two named sources of confusion
questions.why:
The two named sources of confusion are hazardous homophones, words that sound alike but differ in meaning and so mislead a listener, and ambiguity, a word, phrase or sentence open to more than one interpretation.

Denotation and connotation are the two levels of word meaning, not sources of confusion; slang, jargon, accent and dialect are not among the named pair.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six competencies attached to the study of communication and meaning?
questions.why:
The six are Semiotic Awareness, Contextual Interpretation, Clarity in Expression, Active Listening, Conflict Resolution and Cultural Sensitivity.

Persuasive Writing belongs to the language-skills lesson (with Active Listening, Effective Speaking, Reading Comprehension and Critical Thinking), not to this one.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about meaning in communication is correct?
options: Meaning is constructed by the listener through active interpretation
Meaning is fixed by the dictionary and passes unchanged to the listener
Signs and symbols carry no meaning unless words accompany them
Connotation is stable across cultures while denotation varies
questions.why:
Meaning is multifaceted and requires active interpretation by the listener, who must consider context and recognise possible ambiguities.

The dictionary gives only denotation, so the second statement ignores connotation; signs and symbols carry meaning without words, which is the point of semiotics; and it is denotation that is stable and connotation that varies with culture, so the last statement is reversed.

questions.q: By structure, classify this sentence: 'Bisi, while the rain poured, finished the report.'
questions.why:
One independent clause (Bisi finished the report) plus one dependent clause (while the rain poured) is a complex sentence. A subordinate clause may sit first, last or inside the main clause without changing the label.

Simple ignores the 'while' clause; compound needs two independent clauses; compound-complex needs two independent clauses as well as the dependent one.

questions.q: By structure, classify this sentence: 'Since the lab was locked, the students waited outside; the technician arrived an hour later.'
questions.why:
Two independent clauses (the students waited outside / the technician arrived an hour later) joined by a semicolon, plus the dependent clause 'since the lab was locked': two or more independent clauses and at least one dependent clause is compound-complex.

Complex misses that the semicolon joins a second independent clause; compound ignores the 'since' clause; simple ignores both.

questions.q: Which of these four sentences is exclamatory?
options: What time does the match start?
The match ended in a draw.
questions.why:
An exclamatory sentence expresses strong emotion and ends with an exclamation mark: 'What a goal that was!'

The first is interrogative (it asks and ends with a question mark), the third imperative (it tells someone to do something), the last declarative (a statement of fact). The two 'What' openers are the trap: a question word does not make the second one a question.

questions.q: How many function words are in the sentence 'The clever boy has quietly buried the bag under the table'?
questions.why:
Function words: the, has, the, under, the = 5 (three articles, an auxiliary verb and a preposition). Content words: clever, boy, quietly, buried, bag, table = 6 (adjective, noun, adverb, verb, noun, noun).

Answering 6 swaps the two classes; 4 treats the auxiliary 'has' as a content verb; 3 counts only the articles.

questions.q: A pronoun such as 'them' points to a thing, and an auxiliary verb such as 'has' looks like a verb. To which word class does each belong?
options: 'them' is a content word, 'has' is a function word
'them' is a function word, 'has' is a content word
questions.why:
Pronouns and auxiliary or helping verbs are both listed among the function words, along with conjunctions, prepositions and articles. Content words are nouns, main verbs, adjectives and adverbs, so only a main lexical verb counts as content.

Calling 'them' content mistakes pointing to a thing for carrying meaning; calling 'has' content mistakes the shape of a verb for a lexical verb; calling both content ignores the class altogether.

questions.q: When 'The girl was chased by a huge dog' is spoken naturally, which words carry the stress?
questions.why:
In English conversation emphasis falls on content words while function words stay unstressed. girl (noun), chased (verb), huge (adjective) and dog (noun) are the content words.

The first option stresses exactly the function words; the third keeps the auxiliary 'was' and drops the main verb; the fourth stresses the preposition 'by' and drops the subject noun.

questions.q: Which of the following sentences applies the rules of concord correctly?
options: The coach and the players is ready.
Neither the players nor the coach are ready.
Either the coach or the players are ready.
The players or the coach are ready.
questions.why:
With 'or' or 'nor' the Rule of Proximity Agreement applies: the verb agrees with the closest subject. In 'Either the coach or the players are ready' the nearest subject is the plural 'players', so 'are' is right.

The first sentence joins its subjects with 'and', which makes a plural subject needing 'are'; in the second and fourth the singular 'coach' is nearest the verb, so both need 'is'.

questions.q: Choose the verb: 'The list of successful candidates ___ on the notice board.'
questions.why:
The subject is 'list', which is singular; 'of successful candidates' is a prepositional phrase, not a second subject, so the number of the subject must match the verb: 'is'.

'are', 'have been' and 'were' all agree with the nearer noun 'candidates', the classic over-application of proximity agreement, which governs 'or' and 'nor', not prepositional phrases.

questions.q: A sentence has two subjects joined by 'or', one singular and one plural. Which rule decides whether the verb is singular or plural?
options: Agreement with the first subject named
questions.why:
The Rule of Proximity Agreement requires the verb to align with the closest subject in a sentence with multiple elements, and the presence of 'or' is what brings it into play.

Agreeing with the first subject ignores proximity; there is no 'coordinating conjunction rule' of concord; tense has nothing to do with number.

questions.q: (1) Some hawk snacks between lectures. (2) Others drive for ride-hailing apps at night. (3) A few tutor secondary-school pupils at weekends. (4) In short, many undergraduates now run small businesses to fund their studies. Which sentence is the topic sentence?
questions.why:
The topic sentence states the main idea of the whole paragraph, and here it comes last: it is usually first, but it can be in the middle or at the end.

Sentences 1 to 3 are supporting details, each one example of the small businesses the fourth sentence names; none of them could stand as a summary of the paragraph.

questions.q: 'The new levy is revenue-neutral; ___, it will not raise the total tax take.' Which transition fits the gap?
questions.concept: Choosing a transition word for the sense
questions.why:
The second half restates the first in plainer terms, which is a Clarification transition: 'in other words', with 'to clarify', 'that is to say' and 'in simpler terms'.

'For example' would have to introduce an instance, not a restatement; 'nevertheless' is Contrast and would signal that the second half cuts against the first; 'meanwhile' is a Time word and would put the two halves side by side in time.

questions.q: Which group contains only Sequence/Order transition words?
questions.concept: Sorting a transition word into its category
questions.why:
First, Next and Finally all mark the order of steps, the Sequence/Order category.

Simultaneously, During and Eventually are Time words; Therefore, Thus and Accordingly are Cause and Effect; Indeed, Certainly and Above all are Emphasis.

questions.q: Which sentence breaks the unity of this paragraph? (1) Exam stress affects many first-year students. (2) Some lose sleep in the week before their papers. (3) The cafeteria now sells jollof rice on Fridays. (4) Others skip meals in order to revise.
questions.why:
Unity requires a single central theme with every sentence relating to it; sentence 3 digresses to the cafeteria menu, and avoiding digression is essential to unity.

Sentence 1 is the topic sentence; sentences 2 and 4 are supporting details about exam stress, so they keep the theme.

questions.q: Which of the following sentences uses the apostrophe correctly?
questions.why:
'students'' shows plural possession, one of the three apostrophe uses (possession, contraction, plural possession).

'it's' means 'it is', so 'it's tail' reads 'it is tail'; 'Its a beautiful day' needs the contraction 'It's'; 'cats tail' needs the singular possessive 'cat's'.

questions.q: 'The conference has speakers from Lagos, Nigeria, Nairobi, Kenya, and Cairo, Egypt.' The list reads as six places. Which mark should separate the three items?
questions.concept: Semicolon in a list with internal commas
questions.why:
A semicolon separates items in a list when the items themselves contain commas: 'Lagos, Nigeria; Nairobi, Kenya; and Cairo, Egypt' now reads as three places.

A colon introduces a list rather than separating its items; a hyphen joins compound words; an em dash sets off an interruption or emphasises information.

questions.q: A student quotes a long sentence but leaves out its middle words. Which punctuation mark shows that words have been omitted?
questions.concept: Ellipsis, brackets and dashes in quotations
questions.why:
The ellipsis marks omitted words in a quotation; its other uses are a trailing-off thought and a pause or uncertainty.

Brackets do the opposite job, enclosing words added to a quotation; an em dash sets off information within a sentence; a hyphen joins compound words or breaks a word at a line end.

questions.q: An essay first sets out why the fuel subsidy was removed and then traces the rise in transport fares that followed. Which of the eleven writing strategies is it using?
questions.why:
Cause and effect traces why something happened and what followed from it, which is exactly the subsidy-to-fares link.

Problem-solution would go on to propose remedies; chronological order arranges events by time without linking them as cause and result; comparison sets out similarities between two things.

questions.q: Which of the following gives a paragraph coherence?
options: Cohesive links such as conjunctions and pronouns that connect the ideas in logical order
A single central theme that every sentence relates to
A topic sentence placed at the very start
questions.concept: Unity versus coherence in a paragraph
questions.why:
Coherence is orderly, logically connected ideas held together by cohesive links like conjunctions and pronouns, so the paragraph flows smoothly; it is a matter of joins, not of facts.

A single central theme is unity, a different component; the topic sentence need not be first; sentence length has nothing to do with it.

questions.q: Before interviewing market traders for a feature article, a reporter writes down the questions he intends to ask. Which pre-writing technique is this?
questions.concept: Naming a pre-writing technique from a scenario
questions.why:
Drafting questions is preparing the questions in advance so that the relevant topics are covered and essential information is secured; the journalist before an interview is its signature case.

Research gathers information from sources; listing enumerates items to guide structure; outlining sets out key points and their flow for the piece itself.

questions.q: A poet writes 'harmattan' in the middle of a page and jots around it every word and image the season brings to mind. Which pre-writing technique is this?
questions.concept: Naming a pre-writing technique from a scenario
questions.why:
Clustering is associating words or images around a central theme to generate creative ideas, and the poet is its set example.

Outlining fixes sequence and hierarchy; storyboarding plans a sequence of scenes visually; free-writing is continuous unstructured prose, not words arranged round a core.

questions.q: A novelist writes continuously for twenty minutes without stopping to correct or organise anything, in order to discover what her character really wants. Which pre-writing technique is this?
questions.concept: Naming a pre-writing technique from a scenario
questions.why:
Free-writing is unstructured, continuous writing that turns up unexpected details and insights, such as a character's backstory or motivation.

Brainstorming produces a list of ideas or topics rather than a flow of prose; outlining fixes sequence before writing; research gathers information from outside sources.

questions.q: Kemi reads through her finished essay, moves its third paragraph ahead of the second and rewrites the introduction so that it previews the argument properly. Which post-writing activity is this?
questions.why:
Revision works at the level of content and structure: revisiting the introduction and reorganising paragraphs are its two named examples.

Proofreading catches only typos, misspellings and punctuation; editing changes grammar and sentence structure; polishing transitions smooths the joins between paragraphs without moving them.

questions.q: Tunde sets his essay's font to 12 point, its margins to one inch and its lines to double spacing. Which post-writing activity is this?
questions.concept: Naming a post-writing activity from a scenario
questions.why:
Formatting and presentation is the activity that sets font size, margins and spacing for professionalism and visual appeal.

Proofreading deals with textual errors, not layout; publishing or submitting is the final hand-over; finalising conclusions rewrites the closing paragraph.

questions.q: Put these post-writing activities in the order they should be done: (1) proofread for typos and punctuation; (2) reorganise the paragraphs; (3) submit the essay to the instructor; (4) correct grammar and sentence structure.
questions.why:
Revise (content and structure) first, then edit (grammar and sentence structure), then proofread (surface slips), and finally publish or submit, which marks the end of the writing process: 2, 4, 1, 3. Big changes, then medium, then small, then out the door.

4, 2, 1, 3 edits sentences that may then be moved or cut; 2, 1, 4, 3 proofreads before editing, so new errors go uncaught; 1, 4, 2, 3 proofreads first, wasting the pass.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the ten pre-writing activities?
questions.why:
The ten pre-writing activities are brainstorming, freewriting, research, mind mapping, outlining, identifying audience and purpose, storyboarding, drafting questions, clustering and listing.

Peer review, exchanging drafts with a peer for feedback, is a post-writing activity; it needs a draft to exist first.

questions.q: Revising the argument, editing for grammar, proofreading for typos and checking citations all belong to which stage of the writing process?
options: Publishing, which is a fourth stage of its own
questions.why:
Post-writing is everything undertaken after the initial draft: revision, editing for grammar and style, peer review, proofreading, checking citations, polishing transitions, formatting, finalising conclusions and finally publishing or submitting.

Pre-writing precedes composition (brainstorming, outlining, research); during-writing is the drafting itself; and publishing or submitting is the last post-writing step, not a fourth stage.

questions.q: Bola starts writing her summary before working out what the author's primary argument is, so it lists points without showing which one is central. Which step of summary writing has she skipped?
options: Identify the thesis or main idea
questions.concept: Steps of summary writing applied to a fault
questions.why:
Step 2, identify the thesis or main idea, determines the primary argument or message to which everything else is subordinate; without it the summary cannot show what is central.

She did read the text (step 1); highlighting key points (step 3) picks the supporting details, which presupposes a known main idea; condensing (step 4) concerns own words and brevity.

questions.q: A letter reads: 'Dear Mrs Okafor, I hope this letter finds you well. I am writing to request a reference for my scholarship application.' Which of the five key parts of a letter is 'I hope this letter finds you well'?
questions.why:
The five key parts are greeting, opening sentence, purpose of the letter, closing and signature. 'I hope this letter finds you well' is the opening sentence.

'Dear Mrs Okafor' is the greeting; 'I am writing to request...' states the purpose of the letter; the closing is the polite sign-off such as 'Yours sincerely'.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the nine steps of letter writing?
questions.why:
The nine steps are identify purpose and audience, choose the right format, greeting, introduction, body, politeness and tone, closing, closing salutation, and review and edit.

Presenting methodology is a step of report writing; a letter has no methodology section.

questions.q: A paragraph of a report explains that its data came from a systematic review of statistical agencies, research institutions and NGOs, whose own methods were critically evaluated. Which section of the report is this?
questions.why:
The methodology presents the methods used to gather data, ensuring transparency and reliability; describing which sources were reviewed and how they were evaluated is exactly that.

The introduction states topic, purpose and scope; findings present the results with supporting evidence; conclusions interpret what the findings mean.

questions.q: Put these report-writing steps in the order they are carried out: (1) draw conclusions; (2) present methodology; (3) define the purpose; (4) make recommendations.
questions.concept: Ordering the steps of report writing
questions.why:
Define the purpose comes first (step 1 of eleven), present methodology is step 5, draw conclusions step 7 and make recommendations step 8: 3, 2, 1, 4.

2, 3, 1, 4 gathers data before knowing the purpose; 3, 1, 2, 4 draws conclusions before the methods and findings exist; 3, 2, 4, 1 recommends before concluding, but recommendations must be based on the conclusions.

questions.q: Which term names a written message addressed to a specific person or group, following a formal or informal format, used to convey information, express feelings, make requests or maintain connections?
questions.why:
A letter is a written message or communication addressed to a specific person or group, in a formal or informal format, serving to convey information, express thoughts or feelings, make requests, or establish and maintain connections.

A report is a formal document presenting detailed information, analysis, findings and conclusions on a topic; a summary is a condensed version of a larger text; an essay is not one of the three writing types defined here.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a summary from a report?
options: A summary condenses one source text and adds nothing; a report is generated by the writer's own research
A summary is always longer than a report
A report quotes its sources freely, while a summary must add the writer's own opinion
A summary contains recommendations; a report does not
questions.why:
A summary is a condensed and concise version of a larger text, highlighting its main ideas without adding anything; a report presents the writer's own research, with methodology, findings, conclusions and recommendations that exist in no source text.

A summary is shorter, not longer; a summary must be in the writer's own words and carries no opinion; recommendations belong to the report, not the summary.

questions.q: Which step is common to the procedures for writing a summary, a letter and a report?
options: A final review and revision for clarity, coherence and accuracy
questions.concept: The common final step of summary, letter and report
questions.why:
All three procedures end with the same step: review and revise (or review and edit) for clarity, coherence and accuracy, checking that the piece achieves its purpose.

Identifying purpose and audience opens the letter steps and defining the purpose opens the report steps, but the summary steps begin with reading the text; methodology belongs only to the report; highlighting key points only to the summary.

questions.q: Before reading a history chapter in detail, Tunde spends four minutes on the chapter title, the subtitles and the captions under the illustrations. What is the intended output of this stage?
options: Answers to the questions he has generated
A sense of the text's structure and main ideas
A spoken restatement of the key concepts
A written outline for long term retention
questions.why:
Survey is a fast scan of the whole text before any detailed reading, and all it is meant to yield is an overview: the structure and the main ideas.

Answering the questions you generated is the Read stage, saying the key points aloud is Recite, and building an outline for lasting retention is Review.

questions.q: A chapter ends with ten review questions. Uche answers those ten questions immediately after skimming the headings, and calls this the Question stage of SQ3R. What has he got wrong?
options: The Question stage means generating your own questions, not answering the book's
The Question stage comes after Read, not before it
The Question stage requires the answers to be spoken aloud
The Question stage requires written summaries and outlines
questions.why:
At the Question stage you ask, you do not answer. The questions are your own, generated from what the survey turned up, and they guide the reading that follows.

Question is the second stage and does come before Read; speaking key points aloud is Recite; producing summaries or outlines is Review.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five stages of SQ3R?
questions.why:
The five stages are Survey, Question, Read, Recite and Review. Recall is not one of them, though it is the word most often substituted for Recite.

Survey, Recite and Review are all genuine stages, so choosing any of them means the acronym has not been learned.

questions.q: In the sentence 'The soup was so insipid that Ada reached for the salt and the pepper before her second spoonful', a reader works out that insipid means lacking flavour. Which strategy has the reader used?
questions.why:
Context clues are hints inside the text that let a reader infer the meaning of an unfamiliar word without a dictionary. Reaching for salt and pepper is the clue that fixes insipid as lacking flavour.

An inference draws a conclusion about content rather than the meaning of one word, explicit meaning is what the text states outright, and fact versus opinion sorts verifiable claims from subjective ones.

questions.q: A report contains the sentence 'The company recorded a loss in three consecutive quarters.' A reader who can underline that sentence as the source of the claim is relying on meaning that is:
questions.why:
Explicit meaning is stated directly in the text and requires no inference, and the test is whether you can point to the sentence that says it.

Implicit meaning is suggested and must be inferred, an inference is a conclusion built from stated details plus background knowledge, and subjective belongs to opinion rather than to a stated fact.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is an opinion rather than a fact?
options: Lagos lies in the south west of Nigeria
The new library is the most beautiful building on the campus
Water boils at 100 °C at sea level
questions.why:
A fact is objective and verifiable; an opinion is subjective. Beauty cannot be checked against any record, so the claim about the library is an opinion.

The location of Lagos, the boiling point of water and the start time of an examination can each be verified, which makes all three facts.

questions.q: Which activity belongs to the Review stage rather than the Recite stage?
options: Explaining the key points aloud with the text closed
Skimming the headings and the captions
Building a written outline and returning to it weeks later
Turning the headings into your own questions
questions.why:
Review is written consolidation: summaries, outlines and notes, revisited over time so the material survives to the exam. Recite has no paper; it is retrieval in your own words straight after reading.

Skimming headings and captions is Survey, and turning headings into your own questions is Question.

questions.q: Which of the following defines reading strategies?
options: Techniques and approaches used to enhance comprehension, retention and effectiveness with written text
A systematic five stage method of surveying, questioning, reading, reciting and reviewing
Hints within a text that help a reader infer the meaning of unfamiliar words
Logical conclusions drawn from explicit details plus background knowledge
questions.why:
Reading strategies are the whole category: techniques and approaches that improve comprehension, retention and overall effectiveness with written text, helping a reader process information and extract meaning.

The five stage method is SQ3R, which is only one such strategy; the third option defines context clues and the fourth defines inference.

questions.q: Which term names a logical conclusion drawn from explicit details in a text together with the reader's background knowledge?
questions.why:
An inference is a logical conclusion drawn from details that are stated plus what the reader already knows. It is not a guess, and it can be defended from the text.

An opinion is subjective and needs no textual anchor, a context clue resolves the meaning of one unfamiliar word, and explicit meaning is what the text states outright.

questions.q: Which pair of words were both formed by compounding?
questions.why:
Compounding joins two whole words: rain plus coat, book plus shop. Both source words stay complete and visible.

Brunch and smog are blends made from parts of two words, NASA and laser are acronyms built from initial letters, and sushi and safari are borrowings from other languages.

questions.q: Which of these words was formed by conversion?
options: to text, from the noun text
questions.why:
Conversion changes a word's grammatical category with no affix added at all, as when the noun text is used as the verb to text.

Hopeless adds the suffix less, so it is affixation and derivation; webinar is a blend of web and seminar; danfo is a borrowing.

questions.q: 'ATM' is built from the initial letters of a phrase but is spelled out letter by letter rather than pronounced as a single word. What is it called?
questions.why:
Both acronyms and initialisms are made of initial letters, but an acronym is pronounced as a word, as NASA is, while an initialism is spelled out, as ATM is.

A blend fuses parts of two words and a clipping shortens a single word, and neither uses initial letters at all.

questions.q: Adding the suffix -ness to 'kind' gives 'kindness'. What does the suffix do?
options: Changes an adjective into a noun
Changes a noun into an adjective
Changes a verb into a noun
Leaves the word class unchanged and marks only number
questions.why:
Kind is an adjective and kindness is a noun naming the quality, so -ness moves the word from adjective to noun, as -ity does in ability.

The reverse direction would need a suffix such as -ful, -er in teacher is what turns a verb into a person noun, and marking number is inflection rather than derivation.

questions.q: Which of these endings creates a new dictionary word rather than only marking grammar?
questions.why:
A derivational affix makes a new word, usually of a new class: simple is an adjective, simplify is a verb, and simplify earns its own dictionary entry.

Plural -s, past tense -ed and -ing are inflectional; they mark number, tense or aspect and leave the word the same lexeme.

questions.q: Which prefix, added to 'lingual', produces a word meaning 'using only one language'?
questions.why:
Mono- means one, so monolingual describes a speaker of a single language.

Bi- means two and gives bilingual, multi- means many and gives multilingual, and inter- means between, as in interdisciplinary.

questions.q: A philosophy course examines what counts as knowledge, where knowledge comes from and how far it can extend. Which academic term names that branch of philosophy?
questions.why:
Epistemology is the branch of philosophy concerned with the nature, origin and scope of knowledge, which is exactly the ground described.

Semiotics studies signs and symbols and their role in communication, pedagogy is the method and practice of teaching, and exegesis is critical explanation or interpretation of a text.

questions.q: 'Advert' was formed by shortening 'advertisement'; 'smog' was formed from parts of 'smoke' and 'fog'. In that order, the two processes are:
questions.why:
Clipping shortens one word without fusing anything, giving advert from advertisement. Blending fuses parts of two words, giving smog from smoke and fog.

Swapping the labels misses that only one source word is involved in advert; compounding would need two whole words, and derivation would need an affix.

questions.q: Which of the following describes vocabulary expansion rather than a word formation process?
options: Attaching a prefix or a suffix to an existing base word
Fusing parts of two words into a single new word
Increasing one's own repertoire of words and expressions in a language
Taking a word from another language into English
questions.why:
Vocabulary expansion is the process of increasing one's repertoire of words and expressions, and it is what a learner does by reading widely, using dictionaries and thesauruses, joining discussions and playing word games.

The other three name ways the language itself builds new words: affixation, blending and borrowing.

questions.q: Asked whether remote work benefits employers, Chidi sets out the savings on office costs, then the supervision problems, and answers the strongest objection before concluding. Which guideline is he following?
questions.why:
Balance means maintaining a balanced perspective by considering different angles or counter arguments where they apply, which demonstrates a nuanced understanding of the topic.

Staying relevant only forbids tangents, elaboration adds depth to a point already made, and providing examples supplies concrete cases, none of which is the same as weighing both sides.

questions.q: Asked about flood control in her city, Halima spends most of her answer describing a holiday she took abroad. Which guideline has she broken?
questions.why:
Staying relevant means keeping focused on the topic and avoiding unrelated tangents, which dilute the impact of the answer. A holiday abroad is a tangent from flood control.

Balance would require counter arguments on the set topic, adapting to the context concerns register and tone, and time management concerns the length of the response.

questions.q: Musa answers in a formal academic assessment using the slang and loose register of a casual chat with friends. Which guideline has he broken?
questions.concept: The Adapt to the Context guideline
questions.why:
Adapting to the context means adjusting the response to the setting, and an academic setting calls for a more formal tone than a casual conversation.

Active listening concerns follow up questions from an interlocutor, concision concerns jargon, pace and enunciation, and concluding effectively concerns the closing summary.

questions.q: Ifeanyi's answer on cross cultural business is well organised and fluent, but every point stays abstract and no company or market is ever named. Which guideline would most improve it?
questions.concept: The Provide Examples and Evidence guideline
questions.why:
Specific examples and evidence illustrate ideas and make a response more convincing, and naming a real company or market is exactly what the abstract answer lacks.

The answer is already organised and already opened, and its fault is missing concreteness rather than a missing counter argument.

questions.q: Given three minutes to answer, Zainab is still developing her second point when the time expires, and no closing summary is ever reached. Which two guidelines has she failed?
options: Understand the Prompt and Organise Your Thoughts
Manage Time Effectively and Conclude Effectively
Adapt to the Context and Practice Active Listening
questions.why:
Managing time effectively means being mindful of the duration and practising answers that are succinct yet comprehensive within the allotted time; concluding effectively means a brief closing summary that reinforces the key message. Both fail here.

Nothing suggests she misread the prompt or wandered off topic, and neither register nor follow up questions are at issue.

questions.q: In the sentence 'I didn't say you should bring coffee', which word must carry the stress to imply that bringing the coffee was optional rather than required?
questions.why:
Stressing should moves the denial onto the obligation itself, so the sentence comes to mean that bringing coffee was never compulsory.

Stressing you implies somebody else should bring it, stressing bring implies you were to do something else with it, and stressing didn't is a flat denial that the words were spoken at all.

questions.q: Saying 'I can't believe you're going to the MOVIES again!' with the heaviest emphasis on the last word conveys:
questions.why:
Placing the emphasis on movies marks that word as the surprising element, so the utterance conveys surprise or disapproval at the repeated trips.

A neutral request would carry no marked emphasis, uncertainty about the destination would need a question, and agreement is the opposite of what the emphasis signals.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes word stress from sentence stress?
options: Word stress falls on a syllable within a word; sentence stress falls on a word within an utterance
Word stress falls on a word within an utterance; sentence stress falls on a syllable
Word stress changes meaning; sentence stress changes only rhythm
Word stress applies to questions only; sentence stress applies to statements
questions.why:
Stress is emphasis on a particular syllable or segment within a word, phrase or sentence. Word stress operates on a syllable inside a word, as in demonstrate; sentence stress operates on a whole word inside the utterance, as in I didn't say you should bring coffee.

The second option reverses the two levels, sentence stress alters meaning as well as rhythm and pronunciation, and neither kind is restricted to one sentence type.

questions.q: 'If the printer is out of paper, the red light comes on. The red light is not on. Therefore the printer is not out of paper.' Which named form is this?
questions.why:
Modus tollens denies the consequent and follows the pattern if A then B, not B, therefore not A. Here B is the red light being on, and denying it yields not A.

Modus ponens would affirm the antecedent, affirming the consequent runs the conditional backwards and is invalid, and a categorical syllogism links classes rather than an if then statement.

questions.q: 'If it is raining, the ground is wet. The ground is wet. Therefore it is raining.' What is wrong with this argument?
options: Nothing is wrong; it is modus ponens
It affirms the consequent, so it is invalid
It denies the antecedent, so it is invalid
questions.why:
The second premise restates the then part of the conditional and the conclusion jumps back to the if part. That is affirming the consequent, a formal fallacy, because a burst pipe would also leave the ground wet.

Modus ponens affirms the if part instead, denying the antecedent negates the if part, and since the form is invalid the question of soundness never arises.

questions.q: From past results and current polling an analyst concludes that Candidate B has a 62 per cent chance of winning. Which type of inductive reasoning is this?
questions.why:
Statistical reasoning draws conclusions from statistical data or probability, and the attached figure of 62 per cent is its signature.

A generalisation is a broad qualitative statement about a group, analogical reasoning argues from similarity between two cases, and modus ponens is deductive rather than inductive.

questions.q: A farmer finds that one maize variety thrives in his soil, and expects a closely related variety with the same requirements to thrive as well. Which type of inductive reasoning is this?
questions.why:
Analogical reasoning draws a conclusion about one case from its similarities to another, and the shared soil requirements are the similarity doing the work.

A generalisation would move from many observed cases to a broad statement, statistical reasoning would attach data or a probability, and enumerative induction generalises about a class from its observed members.

questions.q: 'All metals conduct electricity. Copper is a metal. Therefore copper conducts electricity.' Which named form of deductive argument is this?
questions.why:
A categorical syllogism links classes: a universal claim about metals plus copper's membership of that class forces the conclusion.

Modus ponens and modus tollens both operate on an if then conditional, which this argument does not contain, and a mathematical proof reasons from axioms and the established rules of mathematics.

questions.q: An argument runs: 'My swan is white', then 'Every observed swan is white', then 'Therefore all swans are white'. The middle statement is which stage?
options: Pattern recognition, which supplies the premise
questions.why:
The three stages run specific observation, then pattern recognition which supplies the premise, then general conclusion. Every observed swan is white is the pattern drawn from the observations.

My swan is white is the specific observation, all swans are white is the conclusion, and a counterexample would be a black swan, which is what makes that conclusion false.

questions.q: An inductive argument is never described as valid or invalid. Which pair of words is used of it instead?
questions.why:
Validity is all or nothing and belongs to deductive form. Its inductive counterpart is strength, which comes in degrees and grows with the quantity and quality of the evidence; a strong argument with true premises is cogent.

Truth is a property of statements rather than arguments, sound applies only to deductive arguments, and certain or probable describes conclusions rather than the quality of the argument.

questions.q: Which feature marks an argument as inductive rather than deductive?
options: The conclusion is hedged as likely or probable
The conclusion follows necessarily from the premises
The first premise is an if then conditional
Every one of its premises is actually true
questions.why:
Induction yields conclusions that are probable but never guaranteed, so hedges such as likely, probably, most or a percentage mark it. Deduction yields conclusions that must hold if the premises hold.

Necessity is the deductive test, an if then premise points to modus ponens or modus tollens which are deductive, and the truth of the premises is a separate matter from the type of reasoning.

questions.q: A manager lets each side in a workplace dispute state its concerns without interruption, then helps the two find common ground. Which of the six areas of the importance of listening does this illustrate?
questions.why:
Conflict resolution is the area defined by letting parties express concerns, feelings and viewpoints without interruption and by identifying common ground so a solution can be found.

Building relationships covers trust and rapport in ordinary interaction, effective communication is the general mechanism of responding and questioning well, and leadership effectiveness names outcomes such as morale and informed decisions.

questions.q: A team lead who listens closely to her staff is seen as approachable, makes better informed decisions and lifts morale across the unit. Which area does this illustrate?
questions.why:
Leadership effectiveness names informed decisions, boosted morale, approachability and an inclusive collaborative environment as the payoff of a leader who listens.

Building relationships concerns trust and rapport generally, learning and growth concerns absorbing knowledge and insight, and avoiding miscommunication concerns preventing misunderstanding.

questions.q: A counsellor concentrates on the feelings behind what a client is saying and shows that those feelings are understood. Which listening strategy is this?
questions.why:
Empathetic listening is understanding the speaker's emotions and expressing empathy, which is precisely what the counsellor is doing.

Active listening is demonstrating engagement through full attention, eye contact, nodding and verbal cues; nonverbal communication is reading body language and facial expressions; note-taking records the content.

questions.q: A listener notices that a speaker's folded arms and tight expression do not match his cheerful words. Which listening strategy is at work?
questions.why:
Nonverbal communication as a listening strategy means attending to body language and facial expressions, which is how the mismatch was spotted.

Paraphrasing restates a point in your own words, summarizing condenses the whole, and empathetic listening is about understanding and acknowledging emotion rather than reading posture.

questions.q: Two colleagues act on different understandings of the same instruction because neither listened carefully, and the project is delayed by a week. Which of the six areas does this failure illustrate?
questions.why:
Avoiding miscommunication is the area that names misunderstandings, misinterpretations and conflicts as the cost of poor listening, with serious personal and professional consequences.

Conflict resolution concerns settling a dispute already under way, learning and growth concerns acquiring knowledge, and effective communication describes what good listeners do rather than the failure described.

questions.q: At the close of a two hour meeting, a participant restates the whole discussion aloud in four sentences so everyone leaves with the same picture. Which strategy is this?
questions.why:
Summarizing condenses the whole of what was said into its essentials, which is what a four sentence account of a two hour meeting does.

Paraphrasing restates a single point in your own words, active listening is the broader stance of full attention and engagement, and note-taking would leave a written record rather than a spoken one.

questions.q: After every seminar a student assesses how well she listened and notes down one thing to do better next time. Which case study heading covers this?
questions.why:
Reflective practice is regular self assessment to identify areas for improvement, which is exactly the routine described.

Continuous improvement and critical listening are competencies the lesson claims to build rather than headings of the case study method, and active listening names full attention during the exchange itself.

questions.q: Recognising and respecting communication differences across cultures is named an essential skill for effective listening. Which competence is it?
questions.why:
Cultural competence is the named skill of recognising and respecting communication differences across cultures, and it is called an essential skill for effective listening.

Critical listening is evaluating what is said, empathetic communication responds to the speaker's emotions, and active engagement is demonstrating attention in the exchange.

questions.q: A student rules a narrow left hand column for cues, a wide area on the right for notes, and a band across the bottom filled in shortly after the session. Which note-taking method is this?
questions.why:
The Cornell method divides the page into sections for notes, cues and a summary, its three zones being the cue column, the note taking area and the summaries band, with the summary written shortly afterwards.

Mind mapping produces a visual web rather than a ruled page, bullet points only make notes scannable, and highlighting is a colour cue for key terms.

questions.q: A student draws the central topic in the middle of the page, branches out to subtopics, and branches again to the supporting details. Which technique is this?
questions.why:
Mind mapping creates a visual representation of the content, connecting main ideas to subtopics and supporting details, which is the structure described.

Cornell is a three zone page layout, headings and subheadings impose a linear structure for later retrieval, and bullet points simply make lines scannable.

questions.q: While a colleague describes a problem, Tayo nods, smiles and puts in 'I see' and 'Tell me more'. Which technique for becoming a more active listener is this?
questions.why:
Nodding, smiling and cues such as I see, I understand and Tell me more are the named verbal and non-verbal affirmations, and they encourage the speaker to continue.

Eye contact is a separate technique of its own, an open ended question invites a fuller answer rather than signalling attention, and paraphrasing restates the content for clarification.

questions.q: Instead of asking 'Did the test go well?', a listener asks 'What happened in the test?'. Which technique for becoming a more active listener is this?
questions.why:
An open ended question cannot be closed off with yes or no and invites the speaker to develop the account, which is what the second wording achieves.

Avoiding interruption and minimising distractions govern what the listener refrains from, and eye contact is a non-verbal signal of attention.

questions.q: By listening closely, Amaka grasps not only her colleague's words but the frustration and the intention behind them. Which named benefit of active listening is this?
questions.concept: Benefits of active listening: enhanced understanding
questions.why:
Enhanced understanding is grasping not only the words spoken but the underlying emotions, intentions and context, which is what is described.

Conflict resolution is acknowledging opposing perspectives in a dispute, problem solving is comprehending the details of a problem well enough to offer an informed solution, and note-taking mastery is a listening competency rather than a benefit of active listening.

questions.q: A student adds headings and subheadings to her notes. Which stated benefit does this give?
options: It prevents information overload while writing
It removes the need to review the notes later
It gives an opportunity for clarification with the speaker
It creates a clear structure that makes information easier to find later
questions.why:
Headings and subheadings organise notes into a clear structure, and the stated payoff is that specific information can be found again later.

Preventing information overload is the reason for not writing verbatim, review is still required whatever the structure, and clarification with the speaker comes from paraphrasing and summarising during the exchange.

questions.q: A speaker argues: 'My opponent wants to reduce fuel subsidies, so what he really wants is for Nigerians to suffer.' Which named fallacy is this?
questions.why:
A strawman misrepresents an opponent's position as something weaker or uglier and then attacks that version instead of the real one, which is what turning a subsidy policy into a wish for suffering does.

A hasty generalisation draws a broad conclusion from too few cases, affirming the consequent is a formal fallacy of conditional arguments, and a faulty analogy compares two things alike only in irrelevant respects.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three named importances of active listening?
questions.concept: The three importances of active listening
questions.why:
The three named importances are enhanced understanding, conflict resolution and problem solving. Improved retention is a payoff of combining active listening with note-taking, not one of the three headings.

The other three options are all genuine headings, so choosing any of them means the list has not been learned.
